Need to search first.I've put together verse-by-verse notes for Numbers 16:1–25, but some gaps remain. The search tool hit its usage limit partway through and none of the full pages would load. So everything below comes from the excerpts the searches returned. Each point is in my own words and has its URL.

Nothing turned up from the Lutheran or Pentecostal sites, bibleodyssey.org, oca.org, or any prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are missing. In the sources I did read, the one real disagreement is about church order, under vv. 3 and 10. The notes are thinnest on vv. 11, 13, 17–18 and 20–21.

---

## Numbers 16:1–25: research notes

**v. 1**
- Korah was a Levite from the Kohathite clan, so he was related to Moses and Aaron. Dathan, Abiram and On came from the tribe of Reuben. Constable suggests the Reubenites felt slighted because their tribe had lost the firstborn's rights and wanted a bigger role. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB): Korah's father Izhar was Kohath's second son, yet a man from a younger line had been made chief of the Kohathites (Num 3:30). Resentment over that was probably the root of the revolt. The Reubenites also resented Judah leading the tribes. Their camp was on the same side as Korah's, which made plotting easy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-1.htm
- Ellicott, Gill and Poole note that the Hebrew can be read "Korah… took Dathan and Abiram," making Korah the one who recruited the others. Ellicott adds that we can't say exactly when or where this happened. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-1.htm
- Ellicott calls this the only major event recorded from the long wilderness wandering, and he treats the account as clearly historical. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-16.html
- Mattoon (on Precept Austin) sees two revolts: Korah's against the priesthood and the Reubenites' against Moses as ruler. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik: these 250 well-known leaders didn't start the revolt, but they lacked the discernment to resist Korah and followed him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- Pulpit Homiletics (Binnie) explains their three titles: chiefs of the tribes, members of the national council, and men of reputation. Korah probably made sure every tribe was represented. The book treats this as an organised conspiracy rather than a mob. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm
- Constable: the revolt was started by Levites and leaders, not ordinary people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html

**v. 3**
- Guzik calls this a clever attack. Korah posed as the people's champion while really wanting power. He praised the people's holiness just when the nation was not holy and badly needed strong leaders. Moses never sought his office; God called him to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- Binnie: Korah took a real truth, "a kingdom of priests" (Exod 19:6), and made it a slogan of equality to cover his own ambition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm
- Barnes: Korah didn't want to remove the line between Levites and other Israelites. He wanted the priesthood for himself and his relatives (v. 10). Ellicott thinks Korah claimed a priesthood for all the people, probably hoping to hold the top place in it himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-3.htm
- Coffman: there were two complaints here. Korah's group objected that only the priests could be holy. The Reubenites objected that Moses, a Levite, ruled over them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-16.html
- GotQuestions: the "all are holy" argument was really an accusation against God, who had appointed Moses and Aaron. https://www.gotquestions.org/rebellion-of-Korah.html
- **Where traditions differ (church order):**
  - *Catholic:* writers at Catholic Answers link this verse to Jude 11, which speaks of Korah's rebellion within the church. They argue that if Christians could commit "Korah's rebellion," there must be a ministerial priesthood above the priesthood of all believers. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/more-bible-clues-for-the-priesthood ; https://www.catholic.com/audio/caf/why-have-priests-if-were-all-priests
  - Another Catholic Answers piece describes Korah's attitude as "we're all priests, we don't need this priesthood" and treats it as a warning against causing division. https://www.catholic.com/video/does-god-want-an-organized-religion
  - *Early church:* the Apostolic Constitutions list Korah, Dathan and Abiram among those who caused division and were punished. They say opposing the priesthood deserves heavier punishment than opposing a king. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07156.htm
  - Cyprian says these men tried to make themselves equal to the priest set over them, and the ground swallowing them was God defending his priests. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050664.htm
  - *Protestant reply:* the Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (a Protestant Free Church work) mentions Catholics and "High Church" Anglicans who compared Protestants and Dissenters to Korah. It rejects that reading. In its view, Korah's sin was taking the place of Moses and Aaron, who point ahead to Christ the only mediator. Even Christ didn't take the priesthood until God called him (Heb 5:4–5). So, it argues, the story describes those who set up a human priesthood, not those who reject one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-16.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-27.html
  - The Pulpit Homiletics author "Y." adds that Christians may choose church officers, but the real call comes from Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm

**v. 4**
- Guzik: as in Num 14:5, Moses fell on his face in humble prayer. He did not use his political power or soldiers against the rebels. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- PHC: Moses must have been led to his proposal through prayer. He wouldn't have tried something so bold without God's approval. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-16.html

**v. 5**
- Guzik: after praying, Moses left the decision to God. Even if Korah had a real complaint, a public challenge, accusations and a rival following were the wrong way to handle it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- Ellicott: "tomorrow" literally means "in the morning." The delay may have given On, and Korah's sons, time to back out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-16.html
- Pulpit Homiletics: an honest cause isn't afraid of a trial. Moses allows time and puts the question to God in the plainest way. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: burning incense was the priests' special right and holiest task. The deaths of Nadab and Abihu should have warned Korah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-16.html
- Poole: since you want to be priests, take censers and act as priests, at your own risk. The Cambridge Bible says these censers were the men's own fire-pans, not the tabernacle's sacred utensils. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-6.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: Moses throws Korah's own words from v. 3 back at him. The Levites should have been content with their lower duties in the sanctuary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-16.html
- Precept Austin: Moses already knows whom God will choose. He echoes their phrase back at them, a case of being judged by one's own words (Matt 12:37). https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary

**vv. 8–10**
- Pulpit Commentary: although Moses says "sons of Levi," the speech turns to "you" in the singular, as if Korah alone were truly guilty. JFB praises Moses for being as willing for God's people to be priests as he once was for them to be prophets (Num 11:29). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-8.htm
- Gill: the Levites had been brought near to serve in God's courts and were well provided for by tithes. Poole: priests were few and their privileges large, so the Levites wanted a share. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-10.htm
- Constable, quoting Allen: Korah treated God's call as a privilege rather than a duty of service. Allen warns that heavy talk of "my ministry" can put a person "in Korah's sandals." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/numbers-16.html
- The NET note (quoted on Precept Austin) says Korah wanted to be high priest, something like running in an election with himself as candidate. Korah offers no reply. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary
- Pulpit Homiletics: if we complain about those above us, those below can complain about us. Korah's service was as necessary as Aaron's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm

**v. 11**
- GotQuestions: by revolting against God's appointed leaders, Korah was revolting against God. https://www.gotquestions.org/rebellion-of-Korah.html
- Precept Austin: grumbling against leaders God has appointed is treating God himself with contempt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary

**vv. 12–14**
- Guzik: Dathan and Abiram lied about the past by calling Egypt a land of milk and honey. They expected Moses to have brought them into Canaan already, which was unfair. Their "we will not come" shows they recognised no authority over them. They spoke of Moses as if he were still the proud prince of forty years before. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/numbers/numbers-16.cfm
- Gill, quoted in PHC, says their refusal to come denied Moses' power and despised his authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-16.html
- On "gouge out the eyes" (v. 14), Gill gives two readings. It could be literal: will you be so cruel as to blind us? Or it could mean: will you lead people around like blind men, now toward Canaan, now back toward Egypt? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-14.htm
- PHC: their claim that Moses wanted to kill them in the wilderness was as unjust and false as an accusation could be. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-27.html

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: Moses answers the charge in v. 13 and clears himself of oppression or extortion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-15.htm
- Poole and Gill: his anger was mainly for God's honour, not his own, the kind of anger Christ showed (Mark 3:5). Gill: "not one donkey" means he hadn't taken even the smallest thing from them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-15.htm
- **How different traditions read "Do not regard their offering":**
  - *Reformed (Calvin):* many read this as Moses asking God to show them no mercy. Calvin thinks he only asked God to reject their unclean gift and so punish their ambition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-15.html
  - *Methodist (Wesley):* Moses asks God to reject the coming incense openly. He calls it "their" offering because all the plotters agreed to it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-15.html
  - *Methodist (Adam Clarke):* there was no risk of God accepting it. God never blesses a way of salvation he hasn't appointed himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-15.html
  - *Catholic (Haydock):* Moses' anger was zeal against sin and indignation at the insult to God, as at the golden calf. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-15.html
  - These are differences of emphasis, not real disagreements.

**vv. 16–17**
- Benson, JFB and Gill: "before the LORD" means at the door of the tabernacle, not inside. Only priests could go in, and there the people could watch the test. The Pulpit Commentary says Moses repeats the challenge after the exchange with the Reubenites and adds that Aaron must be there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-16.htm
- *Modern scholarship:* the Cambridge Bible thinks vv. 16–17 repeat vv. 6–7 and were probably added along with vv. 8–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-16.htm
- Guzik: Moses let the rebels take the role they wanted. Two men stood against 250, and God, not popular opinion, would decide. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/

**vv. 18–19**
- Coffman: Korah gathered the people so they would watch what he expected to be his victory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/numbers-16.html
- Precept Austin: the revolt now spreads from a couple of hundred to most of Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary
- JFB: the glory appeared, as when Aaron was installed (Lev 9:23), this time to confirm him in office. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_016.cfm

**vv. 20–21**
- PHC: by rallying to Korah, the people had joined the rebels' cause and shared their guilt, which is why God threatens to destroy them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/numbers-16.html

**v. 22**
- JFB: the prayer is all the more striking because Moses and Aaron are praying for their enemies. Spurgeon (on Precept Austin) praises how quick they were to intercede and how free from revenge. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Num/Num_016.cfm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/numbers-16-commentary
- Guzik: their love for undeserving people shows them being shaped toward Christ's likeness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- **"God of the spirits of all flesh":**
  - Poole: God as Maker of spirits, so Moses is in effect saying "don't destroy your own work." God also knows who acted out of malice and who was simply misled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-22.htm
  - Gill: God made both body and spirit and knows every heart. He compares the plea to Abraham's in Gen 18:25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-22.htm
  - Kingcomments: the title shows God knows everything about the human heart, mind and will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/numbers-16.html
  - *Methodist (Adam Clarke):* the phrase shows the Old Testament treats humans as flesh plus a separate, immortal spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-22.html
  - *Reformed (Calvin):* he discusses the grammar, reads the repeated word for God as adding force, and translates it as God of the spirits "in" all flesh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-22.html
  - Prout (Pulpit sermon) separates two things. The direct punishment of sin falls only on the guilty. Its side effects can fall on the innocent, as with Dathan's children. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/prout/the_god_of_the_spirits_of_all_flesh.htm
- **"One man":** Guzik, Poole and Gill take it to mean Korah, the ringleader. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-22.htm
- *Modern scholarship:*
  - The NET note says the phrase "God of the spirits of all flesh" is difficult. It also appears in later Jewish writings, so some scholars think it was added late. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Num+16%3A21%2C22%2C46-48
  - The same note says Moses' appeal amounts to "better one man die for the nation" (compare John 11:50). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/passage.php?passage=Num+16%3A21%2C22%2C46-48
  - The Cambridge Bible thinks belief in one God for all people comes from the "priestly writer," and that "one man" shows Dathan and Abiram weren't part of that strand of the story. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-22.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- Guzik: the warning to move away was God's mercy, so the people wouldn't be caught in the coming judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/
- Ellicott: it is hard to say what "tabernacle/dwelling" (*mishkan*) of Korah means here and in v. 27. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/numbers-16.html
- Binnie compares the command to separate with Rev 18:4. Matthew Henry: anyone who wants to avoid dying with sinners must come out from among them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/numbers/16.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/numbers/16-27.html

**v. 25**
- Guzik: Moses went to Dathan and Abiram because they refused to come to him. Having the elders follow him was powerful, since they had been appointed to share his load and his vision. Guzik's reference to "Numbers 10:14-27" seems to be a typo for Numbers 11. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/numbers-16/

**Source theories (modern scholarship)**
- The Cambridge Bible thinks two accounts were combined: an older "JE" story of the Reubenites' revolt and a "priestly" story of Korah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-1.htm
- On the same page, another commentator (unnamed in the excerpt) replies that even if the story was expanded somewhat clumsily, that doesn't affect its truth or inspiration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/numbers/16-1.htm
